summary: This informational memo sets terminology for benchmarking eBGP convergence in the control plane of a single BGP device. It is meant to standardise how the methodology is described, with later documents covering other aspects.

eli5.summary: Before timing how fast a router updates its routes, everyone must use the same words. This is the word list for BGP.

questions: how to measure bgp convergence speed
what is a bgp route instance
subtitle: Standard terminology for measuring how quickly routers update their routing tables.

tldr.problem: When testing how fast routers converge to consistent routing information after topology changes, different vendors used different terminology and measurement approaches, making it hard to compare results.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines standardized terms for all the concepts involved: routing data structures (RIBs, FIBs, prefixes), the types of route changes, and what convergence means for a single device's control plane.
tldr.outcome: The standard terminology allows benchmark testing to be conducted consistently and comparisons to be meaningful. This is the foundation for later methodology documents that will describe actual test procedures.

facts.label: MRAI timer
facts.value: Minimum interval between route advertisements for a single prefix

facts.label: MAOI timer
facts.value: Minimum interval between locally originated route advertisements

facts.label: Route instances factor
facts.value: 4 to 10 times the number of unique routes in a large router

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Single BGP device control plane, eBGP convergence

today: RFC 4098 remains the standard terminology reference for BGP convergence benchmarking. It has not been obsoleted and is used as the foundation for ongoing research and vendor benchmarking in routing protocol performance.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC establishes standard terminology for benchmarking the convergence of BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) routing processes in individual routers. The problem it solves is clear: when vendors, researchers, and operators test how quickly routers converge after topology changes, they each use different terms and measure different things, making it impossible to compare results fairly.

The document focuses on the control plane—how routing information is processed and propagated—rather than the data plane (packet forwarding). It covers eBGP (external BGP, used between different autonomous systems) and defines the measurement terms at the foundation level before later documents define the actual test methodology.
sections.eli5: Imagine timing how fast runners run, but each person uses different words to describe the race and different places to measure. This memo picks the same words and rules for everyone.

sections.title: Routing Information and Data Structures
sections.content:
The RFC defines the basic units and containers: a prefix is a contiguous set of address bits (like 192.0.2.0/24); a route combines a prefix with a next hop and other attributes; and an NLRI (Network Layer Reachability Information) is how BGP advertises this in UPDATE messages.

Three key storage structures are defined: the Adj-RIB-In (routes received from peers), the Loc-RIB (the local decision point after policy is applied), and the Forwarding Information Base (FIB, what the data plane uses to forward packets). Understanding which data structure converges at which point is essential for measuring convergence correctly.
sections.eli5: A route is like a road sign: it says 'to reach this place, go this way.' A router keeps multiple lists of signs—what it heard, what it decided to use, and what it tells the forwarder.

sections.title: Route Categories and Device Types
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes between active routes (those that have a corresponding FIB entry) and unique routes (a prefix with only one route instance across all adjacent RIBs) versus non-unique routes (the same prefix available from multiple peers). A single router may have four to ten times as many route instances as unique routes because alternative paths exist.

Router types are classified by their position and role: Provider Edge Routers connect customer networks, Core Routers carry transit traffic, and Inter-provider Border Routers sit at the Internet backbone. The characteristics of convergence differ for each class depending on how many routes and peers they manage.
sections.eli5: Some routers are at the edge, some are in the middle. A big router might know the same destination multiple ways, but only use one path at a time.

sections.title: Timers and Update Behavior
sections.content:
Two critical timers control BGP behavior: the MRAI (MinRouteAdvertisementInterval), which sets the minimum time between route advertisements for a single prefix from one device, and the MAOI (MinASOriginationInterval), which controls how often locally originated routes are advertised. Both use random jitter to avoid synchronization across a network.

The RFC also defines hard reset (complete re-initialization of routing tables after a session failure) and soft reset (re-establishing peering without stopping traffic). Understanding these events is critical because they drive the convergence tests that measure how quickly the device responds to each.
sections.eli5: Routers have speed limits on how fast they tell neighbors about changes. They add randomness so everyone doesn't shout at the same time.

sections.title: Convergence Definition and Measurement Factors
sections.content:
The core definition: a device converges when it has performed all control-plane actions needed to react to topology changes. For BGP, this means when a route change is advertised to downstream peers, not when the change is simply processed internally. This is much stricter than simply running the route selection algorithm.

Many factors affect convergence speed: the number of peers, the number of routes per peer, policy processing complexity, interaction with IGPs (Interior Gateway Protocols), flap damping, and even lower-layer protocol behavior. The RFC catalogs these but notes that a baseline measurement must isolate the core BGP performance first before adding realistic complexity.
sections.eli5: The router is 'done' when it has told its neighbors about the change, not when it first heard about it. Many things can slow this down—too many neighbors, too much filtering, flapping routes.
